clue.text: Most of Italian wine left in church for man on board

indicators.note: in places the wine and the left marker inside the abbreviation for church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is kept

parts.note: Asti is a sparkling wine from Piedmont
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A churchgoer is offered most of a bottle of Italian wine left behind in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' sounds like a sailor, but the board is a chessboard; Asti is a sparkling wine from Piedmont.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle, or rook, is one of the chess pieces, a man on the chessboard.

clue.text: Company to write to US golfer for capital

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
to pen is to write
Walter Hagen was an American golf champion

explanation.surface: A firm writes to an American golfer asking for funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like money for the company; it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Copenhagen is the capital city of Denmark.

clue.text: Little square by shopping centre

parts.note: S is short for square, as in street names
a mall is a shopping centre

explanation.surface: A tiny town square next to a shopping centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Small and little are straightforward synonyms for slight in size.

clue.text: Lengthen lease, in writing

parts.note: to let a property is to lease it
something put down is recorded in writing

explanation.surface: A tenant asks for the rental agreement to be extended, with everything in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lengthen lease' reads as one phrase about a tenancy, but the definition is the single first word.
explanation.definitionFit: To let down a hem or a garment is to make it longer by releasing the turned-up fabric.

clue.text: Shaken, note, kept in school about it

parts.note: A is a note of the musical scale

indicators.note: about means going around, so the school punishment wraps around the little word it

parts.note: a pupil who is gated is confined to school as a punishment
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pupil, shaken by a note, is held back in detention.
explanation.walkthrough: To be gated is British school slang for being kept in as a punishment; IT goes inside after its first letter, giving G-IT-ATED after the note A.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone agitated is disturbed and upset, the emotional sense of being shaken.

clue.text: Expression of surprise from British general and playwright

parts.note: General Charles Gordon died at Khartoum in 1885
Alan Bennett is an English playwright

explanation.surface: A gasp of astonishment from a famous soldier and a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Bennett! is a mild British exclamation of astonishment, named after an American newspaper owner.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mild British exclamation used to show amazement or exasperation.

clue.text: Speak badly of a duke during ceasefire

indicators.note: during means within the time of, so one item sits inside the other

parts.note: a truce is a halt to fighting
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: Someone slanders a nobleman while hostilities are paused.
explanation.walkthrough: A and D go together inside TRUCE, between its R and U.
explanation.definitionFit: To traduce is to slander or malign someone, to speak ill of them.

clue.text: Steaks done differently in Loire town

indicators.note: differently means in another way, so these letters take another order
in places the rearranged letters inside the name of the French town

parts.note: Tours is a city on the Loire in France
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A French restaurant in the Loire valley cooks its steaks in another style.
explanation.definitionFit: Tournedos are small round thick steaks cut from the beef fillet.

clue.text: In conference, pass on piece of tittle-tattle

parts.note: to pass on is to die

indicators.note: a piece of a word is just a fragment of it, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of tittle-tattle

explanation.surface: At a meeting, someone passes along a bit of gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass on' seems to mean relay the gossip, but here it means to die.
explanation.definitionFit: A diet is a formal legislative assembly or conference, as in the Japanese Diet or the Diet of Worms.

clue.text: Artisan needs Band-aid, then emergency room

parts.note: a sticking plaster is a small adhesive dressing
ER is the abbreviation for emergency room

explanation.surface: An injured craftsman needs a bandage and then a trip to hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: A plasterer is a skilled tradesman who applies plaster to walls and ceilings.

clue.text: Meals on wheels provider?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: the charity service delivering hot food to elderly people at home
setter's reading: something serving meals while it rolls along on wheels, on a train

explanation.walkthrough: Meals on Wheels is a well-known British service bringing cooked food to housebound people; the clue takes the phrase literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A dining carriage on a train serves meals to passengers while the train is moving.

clue.text: A shot to the offside towards point is shrewd

parts.note: taken as written
in cricket a cut is a stroke played square on the off side
E is a compass point, east

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator praises a batsman's clever stroke placed towards the fielding position called point.
explanation.walkthrough: Point is also a cricket fielding position on the off side, which makes the surface hang together; here it is just a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: An acute mind is sharp and perceptive, the same as a shrewd one.

clue.text: Holds file showing monument

parts.note: a nelson is a wrestling hold
a file of soldiers marching one behind another is a column

explanation.surface: An office clerk's folder of papers reveals details of a memorial.
explanation.walkthrough: A full nelson and a half nelson are wrestling holds. Nelson's Column stands in Trafalgar Square, London.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson's Column is the tall memorial to Admiral Nelson in central London, a famous monument.

clue.text: Go over plot with grump

parts.note: to cross is to go over
a patch is a small plot of land

explanation.surface: Someone walks across a vegetable plot accompanied by a bad-tempered neighbour.
explanation.definitionFit: A crosspatch is an irritable, bad-tempered person, a sulky sort.

clue.text: Social worker, woman, returned with an aerial

parts.note: a worker ant lives in a social insect colony

indicators.note: returned means sent back the way it came, so the woman's name is read from end to start

parts.note: a common woman's name

explanation.surface: A council social worker and a female colleague come back with a television aerial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' suggests a council employee, but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An antenna is a rod or wire for receiving radio signals, which is what an aerial is.

clue.text: A poisonous fungus? A lot stood out

indicators.note: out suggests something put out of its usual order or shape

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about a toxic mushroom, then the remark that plenty of them stood out.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that not every toadstool is poisonous.
explanation.definitionFit: A toadstool is the popular name for an inedible or poisonous mushroom.

clue.text: Good mixer has litre in the course of drinking spree

indicators.note: in the course of means during, so one item sits within the other

parts.note: a bender is a drinking binge
L is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: A sociable person drinks a litre during a night out on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good mixer' looks like a sociable person at a party; it is the kitchen appliance.
explanation.definitionFit: A blender is a kitchen machine that mixes and purées food, so it is a mixer.

clue.text: It takes a rum one possibly to sweep one off one's feet

indicators.note: possibly hints that these letters could take another form than the one shown

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: It takes an odd sort of person to sweep someone off their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour someone is to make them fall in love, which is to sweep them off their feet.

clue.text: Rosalind's lover is here in Florida

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the hero of Shakespeare's As You Like It, who loves Rosalind
second meaning: a city in central Florida

explanation.surface: A heroine's sweetheart turns out to be living in the Sunshine State.
explanation.definitionFit: Orlando is both Shakespeare's lovestruck hero and the Florida city famed for theme parks.

clue.text: Sense I'm in dreadful form, pointing to a rival who can't be beaten

definitions.text: a rival who can't be beaten

indicators.note: something in dreadful form is in a bad, disordered state, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sportsman senses he is off form, which points to defeat by an unbeatable opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a long-standing opponent or agent of downfall whom one cannot overcome.

clue.text: Photograph fool having injection

parts.note: a mug is a gullible person
a shot is an injection of a drug

explanation.surface: A silly patient getting a jab has their picture taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A mugshot is a police photograph of a suspect's face.

clue.text: Breakaway movement stopping ruler somehow

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified manner, so the letters can be put in any order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rebel faction somehow halts the reign of a ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: A splinter group is a faction that breaks away from a larger party or organisation.

clue.text: Smell coming from European river, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say, so the river is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: the Oder flows along the German-Polish border

explanation.surface: A stink is said to come off a river on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: An odour is a smell, usually a distinctive or unpleasant one.

clue.text: Vulgar characters involved in foreign affairs

indicators.note: characters involved in means some letters taken from within the following words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Crude characters get mixed up in diplomacy.
explanation.walkthrough: Naff is British slang for tasteless or uncool.
explanation.definitionFit: Naff describes something cheap, tacky and lacking in taste, so vulgar fits.

clue.text: A cereal with fruit?

parts.note: taken as written
corn is a cereal crop

explanation.surface: A breakfast bowl of cereal served with fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the fruit is not one for breakfast: an acorn is the nut of the oak tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically an acorn is the fruit of the oak, a nut held in a cup.

clue.text: Assassin with an open razor

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a murderer who kills by slashing
second meaning: the old-fashioned folding barber's blade

explanation.surface: A killer armed with a straight razor.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a murderous person and a straight razor with a long exposed blade.

clue.text: Crony, Alf, trained in the art of hunting with certain birds of prey

definitions.text: the art of hunting with certain birds of prey

indicators.note: trained means shaped by drilling, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Alf and his pal have been trained in hunting with hawks.
explanation.definitionFit: Falconry is the sport of hunting game with trained falcons and hawks.

clue.text: Stiffness shown by Amber leaving arbitrary tribunal

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so those letters go out of the longer name

parts.note: the Star Chamber was an English court notorious for arbitrary judgments
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman called Amber walks stiffly out of a kangaroo court.
explanation.walkthrough: The Star Chamber was an English court of Tudor and Stuart times, now a byword for arbitrary justice; remove AMBER from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch means formal stiffness of manner, as well as the stuff that stiffens collars.
